---
title: "Preface"
---

This is a short web textbook on the **science of deep learning** — modern AI treated as a *scientific object*, surfaced through controlled synthetic experiments, mechanistic probing, and phenomenology. It is the companion to the experimentalist half of a Harvard Physics graduate course taught from this material; the theoretical half (NTK, neural manifold capacity, high-dimensional geometry) is covered separately and deliberately not duplicated here.

## What this book is

Neural networks as **model organisms.** The guiding methodology — taught in [Chapter 1](chapters/01_intro.qmd) and revisited in the two "Science of DL" chapters ([Chapter 7](chapters/07_scidl_training.qmd) and [Chapter 11](chapters/11_scidl_concepts.qmd)) — mirrors how physicists study biological systems via neuroethology:

1. Notice a phenomenon in a real network.
2. Explore broadly to sharpen the question.
3. Build a synthetic model system you can fully instrument.
4. Run experiments the original network does not allow.
5. Bring the findings back to the original system.

The chapters move through the dominant model classes — image classifiers, sequence models, the transformer, large language models pre- and post-training, diffusion, reinforcement learning, world models — and through two pillar chapters on the phenomenology of *training dynamics* and *concept acquisition*. The final chapter widens the frame to intelligence beyond task-learning: multi-agent dynamics, evolution, open-endedness.

## Who this is for

Physicists comfortable with linear algebra, calculus, probability, and statistical mechanics. No prior ML background is required, but the pace assumes graduate-physics-level fluency with quantitative thinking — the book does not re-derive things you already know.

## What this is not

- **Not a classical-ML survey.** SVMs, kNN, decision trees, kernel methods — covered well elsewhere and skipped here.
- **Not a theory exposition.** Generalization bounds, NTK, capacity calculations — handled by a different course.
- **Not a software tutorial.** PyTorch, JAX, kubernetes, MLOps — recipes, not science.

## Source and contributions

Source for this book lives at [github.com/cfpark00/science-of-dl](https://github.com/cfpark00/science-of-dl). Errata, suggestions, and plot-quality reports are welcome via the issue templates.
